sections.overview: Hagen’s sphinx is a North American hawkmoth whose distribution is centred on the central and eastern United States, where its larval food plant, Osage orange, is established.
sections.identification: The adult is a medium-sized grey-brown sphinx with greenish forewing markings and a conspicuous pale discal spot; the caterpillar varies in colour but bears a long tail horn.
sections.habitat: It occurs wherever Osage orange (Maclura pomifera) grows, including hedgerows, yards, parks and planted areas, so its habitat is often a mixture of natural and human-managed land.
sections.diet: Its caterpillars are host-specialists recorded on Osage orange leaves; unlike the related catalpa sphinx (C. catalpae), which feeds on Catalpa, it has not been shown to use other plants.
sections.behavior: The caterpillars feed mainly at night and hide near the trunk during the day, while adults are attracted to lights during the warm-season flight period.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs on the host plant; mature larvae leave it and pupate in the soil, with the number and timing of broods varying with climate.
sections.ecology: It is one member of the North American genus Ceratomia; its strict dependence on Maclura contrasts with congeners such as C. catalpae, illustrating how close relatives can use different host trees.
sections.conservation: No global extinction-risk assessment was found in the consulted moth references; the species’ close association with a cultivated native tree is not itself evidence of secure populations everywhere.
